messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 44

# Dr. Carlos Mendez

Carlos sits in the office with his hands folded in his lap, his wedding band catching the light as he shifts slightly in his chair. At sixty-two, he carries himself with the measured composure of someone accustomed to being in control—the kind of bearing you develop after thirty-five years of holding people's lives in your hands as a surgeon. But today, there is something fragile beneath that composure, something that cracks when he speaks about the accident.

It was eighteen months ago, a Sunday morning. Carlos had decided to drive up to the cabin in the mountains that he and his wife, María, had owned for twenty years. He was looking forward to the quiet, the solitude. The road was familiar—he'd driven it hundreds of times. He remembers the weather was clear, the sun bright on the windshield. He remembers thinking about a patient he'd operated on the day before, wondering how she was recovering. And then, nothing. A truck had crossed the center line. The collision was violent and immediate.

When Carlos wakes up, he is in a hospital bed, and María is holding his hand. He has a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and a laceration on his forehead that required twelve stitches. The truck driver had fallen asleep at the wheel. For three weeks, Carlos thinks about nothing but the image of the grille of that truck coming toward him, how large it seemed, how impossible it was to avoid. He replays it. He counts the seconds. He wonders what would have happened if he'd left five minutes earlier, five minutes later.

When he returns home, Carlos tries to resume his normal life. He returns to the hospital after eight weeks, against his surgeon's recommendation to take longer. María notices he is different. He is more irritable, quicker to anger over small things. He snaps at the residents during rounds in ways he never has before. He finds himself unable to focus during consultations. His hands, which have never trembled, now shake slightly when he's tired. He tells himself it's just the lingering effects of the trauma, that time will heal it.

But the nightmares persist. Most nights, he dreams he is back in the car, and this time the impact kills him. He wakes gasping, his heart racing, his shirt soaked with sweat. María has learned not to touch him when he wakes—he startles violently, and once he nearly struck her without meaning to. Now she simply sits up and waits for him to orient himself to the present.

Driving has become a different experience entirely. Carlos finds himself gripping the steering wheel with white knuckles, his eyes fixed on the road ahead, hypervigilant to every movement of other vehicles. A car changing lanes makes his heart spike. He avoids highways now, taking only surface streets, even when it adds an hour to his commute. Twice, he has nearly caused accidents because he braked suddenly when another vehicle came too close. He has begun making excuses to María about why they should take her car, why she should drive.

At the hospital, Carlos notices he is becoming more withdrawn. He declines invitations to departmental dinners. He finds himself irritable with colleagues, particularly younger surgeons who seem to take unnecessary risks. He has started having doubts about returning to the operating room, though he hasn't admitted this to anyone. His hands are steady when he operates, but his mind is elsewhere—rehearsing the accident, imagining catastrophes, unable to fully inhabit the present moment where he is supposed to be saving lives.

María watches her husband of thirty-eight years and sees someone she recognizes but doesn't quite know anymore. He is here, but he is also somewhere else, trapped in those few seconds before impact.
